cards.front: What is the difference between LocalDate, LocalTime and LocalDateTime?
cards.back: Date only, time only, and both — none of them carry a time zone or offset
cards.extra: "Local" means "no zone": it is a wall-clock value, not an instant on the timeline.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::05 Date and Time

cards.front: When do you need ZonedDateTime instead of LocalDateTime?
cards.back: When the moment must be unambiguous across zones — scheduling, timestamps, DST-sensitive logic
cards.extra: A LocalDateTime at 02:30 may not exist during a DST jump; a ZonedDateTime resolves to a real instant.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::05 Date and Time

cards.front: What is the difference between Duration and Period?
cards.back: Duration is time-based (hours, seconds); Period is date-based (years, months, days)
cards.extra: Adding a Period of one month to 31 January gives 28/29 February; a Duration of 30 days gives something else.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::05 Date and Time

cards.front: Is DateTimeFormatter thread-safe?
cards.back: Yes — it is immutable, unlike SimpleDateFormat
cards.extra: Build one with ofPattern, share it. Sharing a SimpleDateFormat across threads is a classic corruption bug.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::05 Date and Time

cards.front: What is wrong with using System.currentTimeMillis() to measure elapsed time?
cards.back: It is wall-clock time — it can jump backwards when the system clock is adjusted
cards.extra: Use System.nanoTime() for durations and timeouts; it is monotonic.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::05 Date and Time

cards.front: Which legacy date classes still appear in code?
cards.back: java.util.Date, Calendar, and java.sql.Date/Timestamp
cards.extra: Value types in the java.time API have conversion methods, so legacy boundaries are easy to isolate.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::05 Date and Time

cards.front: What is the difference between Socket and ServerSocket?
cards.back: Socket is the client end of a TCP connection; ServerSocket waits and accept()s connections
cards.extra: The accept loop yields a new Socket per client — each one a separate connection on the server side.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::03 Networking in Java

cards.front: What is DatagramSocket for?
cards.back: UDP: connectionless datagrams with no delivery or ordering guarantee
cards.extra: Lower overhead than TCP; you must handle loss and reordering yourself.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::03 Networking in Java

cards.front: What does InetAddress represent?
cards.back: An IP address — host name resolution plus the numeric address
cards.extra: InetAddress.getByName("example.com") resolves; DNS failures surface as UnknownHostException.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::03 Networking in Java

cards.front: What replaced HttpURLConnection in modern Java?
cards.back: java.net.http.HttpClient, added in Java 11
cards.extra: Async, HTTP/2, and a cleaner API than the URL/URLConnection pair.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::03 Networking in Java

cards.front: What is MessageDigest for?
cards.back: A cryptographic hash: one-way digest of bytes, e.g. SHA-256
cards.extra: Hashing is not encryption — you cannot reverse it. Use it for integrity and password storage (with salt).
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::04 Cryptography

cards.front: What is Cipher for?
cards.back: Encrypting and decrypting with a named transformation like AES/GCM/NoPadding
cards.extra: The transformation string is algorithm/mode/padding; choosing the mode matters as much as the algorithm.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::04 Cryptography

cards.front: What is the difference between KeyGenerator and KeyPairGenerator?
cards.back: KeyGenerator makes symmetric keys (AES); KeyPairGenerator makes asymmetric pairs (RSA)
cards.extra: Symmetric is faster but needs a shared secret; asymmetric solves key distribution.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::04 Cryptography

cards.front: What does Signature do?
cards.back: Signs data with a private key and verifies with the public key
cards.extra: Signing is not encryption: the goal is authenticity and integrity, not secrecy.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::04 Cryptography

cards.front: What is Mac in the crypto API?
cards.back: A Message Authentication Code — keyed hash, e.g. HmacSHA256
cards.extra: Unlike a plain digest, it proves the message came from someone holding the key.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::04 Cryptography

cards.front: What is a KeyStore?
cards.back: A password-protected file holding keys and certificates, managed by keytool
cards.extra: JKS and PKCS12 are the common formats; it is how TLS servers hold their certificate and private key.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::04 Cryptography

cards.front: What does a Class object represent?
cards.back: The runtime description of a type — its name, fields, methods, constructors, annotations
cards.extra: Reflection starts here: obj.getClass(), Type.class or Class.forName(name).
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::21 Reflection

cards.front: What is the difference between getMethods() and getDeclaredMethods()?
cards.back: getMethods() returns public members including inherited ones; getDeclaredMethods() returns only what this class declares, at any visibility
cards.extra: Getting at private members requires the declared variant plus setAccessible(true).
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::21 Reflection

cards.front: How do you bypass private with reflection?
cards.back: field.setAccessible(true) — unless a module or security manager forbids it
cards.extra: That is why strong encapsulation in JPMS exists: it can make this fail rather than silently work.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::21 Reflection

cards.front: How do you create an instance reflectively?
cards.back: clazz.getDeclaredConstructor(...).newInstance(args)
cards.extra: It throws InvocationTargetException wrapping whatever the constructor threw — a frequent source of confusing stack traces.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::21 Reflection

cards.front: What is a dynamic proxy?
cards.back: A runtime-generated class implementing the interfaces you specify, routing every call to an InvocationHandler
cards.extra: The mechanism behind Spring AOP and many mocking frameworks.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::21 Reflection

cards.front: Does reflection see generic type information?
cards.back: Partially — erasure removes it from the bytecode, but signatures of fields, methods and supertypes are retained
cards.extra: getGenericType() reads those signatures. A List<String> field keeps its parameter, a local variable does not.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::21 Reflection

cards.front: What does Class.forName do that getClass() cannot?
cards.back: Loads a class by name at runtime — and by default initialises it
cards.extra: forName(name, false, loader) loads without running static initializers. This is how plugins and JDBC drivers get loaded.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::21 Reflection

cards.front: What does a Locale describe?
cards.back: A language and region combination that drives formatting, parsing and collation
cards.extra: Locale.FRANCE vs Locale.CANADA_FRENCH: same language, different number and date conventions.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::13 Internationalization

cards.front: What is a ResourceBundle?
cards.back: A set of locale-specific property files resolved by name: Messages_fr.properties
cards.extra: Lookup walks from the most specific locale to the default, so you only translate what differs.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::13 Internationalization

cards.front: Why not sort text with String.compareTo across locales?
cards.back: It compares UTF-16 code units, which is not alphabetical order in most languages
cards.extra: Collator.getInstance(locale) does locale-aware ordering — including accents and case rules.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::13 Internationalization

cards.front: Why use NumberFormat instead of String.format for money?
cards.back: It applies the locale's grouping, decimal separators and currency symbol
cards.extra: 1,234.56 in the US is 1.234,56 in Germany — the same number formatted differently.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::13 Internationalization

cards.front: What is ZipFile for versus ZipInputStream?
cards.back: ZipFile opens a random access archive from disk and lists entries; ZipInputStream streams sequentially
cards.extra: The streaming version works on an InputStream and cannot jump backwards.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::02 File Operations

cards.front: How do you create a ZIP archive in Java?
cards.back: ZipOutputStream: put an entry, write bytes, close the entry, repeat
cards.extra: Each entry needs putNextEntry/closeEntry; forgetting the close produces a corrupt archive.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::02 File Operations

cards.front: What is the difference between GZIP and ZIP in Java?
cards.back: GZIP compresses a single stream; ZIP holds many named entries
cards.extra: GZIPInputStream has no entry structure, which is why it is used for single files and HTTP bodies.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::02 File Operations
